entries.english:
Co-plaintiff/applicant/intervenor: Rudolf von Hürnheim zu Jettenhofen (spelled Uettenhofen and Uttenhofen in the case record), councillor and household steward to the Fürstbischof von Eichstätt and administrator at Obermässing. Co-defendants/intervenors: Kurfürst Friedrich III von der Pfalz, his governor and councillors at Amberg, Georg Thomas von Wildenstein, and Hans Hertl (usually Hertlin in the record), Palatine Schultheiß or judge at Neumarkt. Plaintiff’s counsel: Dr. Paul Haffner (1575) and Dr. Philipp Seiblin (1577). Defendants’ counsel: (Dr. Johann) Deschler and (Dr. Heinrich) Burckhardt (1562), and Dr. Christoph Reiffsteck (1576).

The contemporary case caption is *mandatum et citatio* concerning six detained subjects at Griesbach and Obernried; the modern description identifies the dispute as the right to collect taxes from Hürnheim subjects. In 1561 the Palatine government at Amberg levied the Palatine land tax for the first time. Rudolf refused to pay, and co-defendant Hans Hertl, judge at Neumarkt, imprisoned six of Rudolf’s subjects at Obernricht (called Obernried in the case) and Burggriesbach (called Griesbach in the case) for refusing the tax. Before the Imperial Chamber Court, Kurfürst Friedrich denied Rudolf’s imperial immediacy, arguing that he was a Palatine subject and that the Kurfürst had territorial and criminal jurisdiction; taxes had long been collected by the Neumarkt office. Rudolf argued that the Jettenhofen manor, with all its courts and rights, belonged to him and that as a member of the Franconian Imperial Knighthood, Altmühl canton, he was exempt from the Elector’s territorial sovereignty. Jettenhofen included two thirds of Burggriesbach and properties acquired by purchase at Schmellnricht (called Schmellenried[t] or Niederriedt in the file), Obernricht, Höfen, and Lauterbach. Rudolf acknowledged that the Kurfürst held criminal jurisdiction over Burggriesbach, acquired only in 1523 under an agreement with Hochstift Eichstätt. On 27 January 1585 the Imperial Chamber Court prohibited the defendant from interfering with the plaintiff’s right to collect taxes or disturbing his tax exemption. Proceedings before that court are recorded for 1562–1615, especially 1571–1578.

A Hürnheim commission file, submitted 27 October 1572, contains testimony taken before an imperial commission in 1571. Enclosures to the missing plaintiff’s petition include: (A, C, D) 1530 fief charters from Markgraf Georg von Brandenburg-Ansbach und Brandenburg-Kulmbach, Herzog Wilhelm V von Bayern, and Bischof Gabriel von Eichstätt to the brothers Johann Sebastian, doctor of laws, Walter, Rudolf, Hieronymus, and Bero von Hürnheim, concerning Burggriesbach and Schmellnricht, four farms and two smallholdings at Obernricht, and Jettenhofen Castle; (B) the 1472 agreement between Stephan Schenk von Geyern zu Jettenhofen and Hans von Reichenau on the church-fair rights and *Ehaft* at Burggriesbach; (E) the 1530 purchase agreement between brothers Konrad and Philipp von Rosenberg and the Hürnheim brothers for Jettenhofen Castle and its properties and rents; (F) the Rosenberg brothers’ rent book of 1530; notices of meetings of the Franconian Imperial Knighthood, Altmühl canton (1532–1573); (G) the 1531 purchase agreement by which Georg Plab and Hans Nuber, guardians of Hermann Mich(t)ner’s orphaned children, all citizens of Hilpoltstein, sold Burggriesbach Castle and fortress to the Hürnheim brothers; and (H) an extract from the agreement of 1523 among Kurfürst Ludwig V von der Pfalz, his brother Pfalzgraf Friedrich, and Bischof Gabriel von Eichstätt, made before Georg von Heideck as presiding arbitrator, Albrecht von Wildenstein zu Breitenegg, and Kaspar Adelmann von Adelmannsfelden, canon and cathedral custodian of Eichstätt. That agreement concerns boundaries of the Neumarkt office, Berngau manor, and the Holnstein, Hirschberg, Greding, and Berching offices and courts, as well as high jurisdiction, tax collection, and the hunting ban there; the extract was also submitted on 20 October 1574. (J) Extracts from Eichstätt’s criminal court book (1512 and undated). The register dates the beginning of the proceedings to 1562.
